name: Reciprocity
description: People feel obligated to return favors, gifts, or concessions — including small, unsolicited ones — which increases compliance with a subsequent request.
design_relevance_note: The theoretical basis for free samples, unexpected small gifts with purchase, and 'give value first' onboarding/marketing patterns.
prevalence_note: One of Cialdini's six core principles, taught in essentially every persuasion-design or marketing curriculum.

findings.description: In two restaurant field experiments, servers who gave diners an unexpected small gift (candy/mints) along with the check received higher tip percentages than servers who gave no gift — and the amount and manner of the gift mattered (per secondary characterization: roughly +3% for one mint, tips roughly quadrupling to ~14% for two mints given individually rather than together). Reciprocity was argued to be a stronger explanation than mood or impression-management effects.
findings.source_title: Sweetening the Till: The Use of Candy to Increase Restaurant Tipping

applications.title: A 139,000-person field experiment finds reciprocity signaling didn't move voter turnout
applications.description: J-PAL researchers partnered with the Colorado Civic Engagement Roundtable to test whether offering a follow-up reminder call during an initial voter-mobilization call -- a signal of good will meant to invoke reciprocity -- would make a subsequent reminder call more effective at increasing turnout. In a randomized field experiment covering 139,153 individuals across five treatment arms and a control group during the 2014 Colorado midterms, attempting any late reminder call increased turnout by 1.2 percentage points among people successfully reached earlier -- but explicitly offering that follow-up as a reciprocity-invoking gesture in the first call made no additional difference over an unannounced reminder call. The researchers concluded reciprocity likely played a smaller role in voter mobilization than the underlying theory predicted.
applications.industry_context: political campaigning / voter mobilization, nonpartisan civic engagement
applications.ethical_note: A randomized academic field study of nonpartisan civic-engagement calls with a publicly disclosed null result on the specific reciprocity mechanism being tested -- no manipulation of voters beyond a standard get-out-the-vote call, and the honest negative finding is the notable part.

applications.title: BIT's field experiment: a free packet of sweets significantly increased large charitable donations -- but the effect halved on repeat exposure
applications.description: In two large UK field experiments, the Behavioural Insights Team gave passersby a small gift (a packet of sweets) before asking them to donate an average of GBP515 to charity. People who received the sweets were significantly more likely to donate than those given only a flier or nothing at all. When the same participants were approached a second time with the same gift, the reciprocity effect fell by more than half -- though it remained net financially positive for the charity.
applications.ethical_note: A genuine test of reciprocity's real-world durability, not just its existence -- directly useful for any product or campaign relying on a 'free gift' or 'unlock' to drive a later ask (a free trial extension, a bonus feature), since this study honestly shows the effect meaningfully decays with repetition rather than remaining constant, a caution against assuming a reciprocity-based tactic scales linearly with reuse.

applications.title: The Nielsen Company showing report content before requesting contact information
applications.description: The Nielsen Company shows a brief preview article summarizing a report's findings before asking a user for contact information to access the full document -- providing real value first, then making a request, in the sequence the reciprocity principle describes as more effective and more fair.
applications.ethical_note: Genuinely providing value before requesting something in return is the reciprocity principle's own honest form -- no deception, no unrequited cost placed on the user first. Paired directly with the comScore entry in this same wave to show the same principle applied well versus applied backwards, since the source itself frames them as a direct before/after contrast.

applications.title: Whatley et al. (1999): reciprocity weakens sharply once a favor is given anonymously
applications.description: In an experiment testing how internalized the norm of reciprocity really is, people who received a favor were less likely to comply with a later donation request specifically when they were not required to put their name on the compliance form -- removing the social visibility of the exchange substantially weakened the reciprocal obligation people otherwise felt.
applications.ethical_note: A finding about the social-visibility precondition for reciprocity to function, not itself a designed influence on a user -- directly relevant to online product design, where most reciprocal exchanges (a free trial, an unlocked feature, free content) happen in exactly the low-visibility, low-social-pressure conditions this study found weaken the reciprocal obligation, which may explain why 'give first, ask later' strategies work less reliably online than the in-person literature would predict.

applications.title: comScore requiring contact information before releasing a free report
applications.description: comScore asks users to submit their contact information before granting access to a free report, requesting something from the user (their data) before providing any value in return -- described as inverting the reciprocity principle's usual sequencing rather than applying it.
applications.ethical_note: Gating content behind a contact form is a standard, widely accepted lead-generation practice, not inherently deceptive -- but NN/g's own framing treats asking before giving as a real trust cost, not a neutral business choice. Graded mixed rather than manipulative_risk since nothing about the practice is dishonest, and rather than user_beneficial since it does place a real cost on the user before any value is delivered. Directly contrasted with the Nielsen Company entry in this same wave, which the source itself frames as the preferable alternative.
